# What goes in a column

So far a new column has been arithmetic on the ones already there. This part
is about everything else you can put in one: text you need to clean up, a
number that arrived as text, a date you want the year out of, and a category
that depends on a condition. Missing values are their own subject, and they
get the closing chapter.

The cell is where grammars usually leak. Most tools keep their verbs small
and then hand the inside of a column to something larger: a regular
expression language for text, a format string for dates, the host language
itself for everything conditional. Each of those is a second grammar hiding
inside the first, and each is a thing you relearn every time you return.

So one law holds this part together: **no new grammar inside a cell**. Every
value in this part is written the same way, as a plain named function inside
`add` or `summarize`, taking columns and giving a column. The words are few
and closed on purpose: a handful of text repairs, four conversions that say
what they give, five date parts, one conditional. When
they are not enough, the answer is the exit shown in [What it wrote](../chapters/what-it-wrote.qmd), not a pattern language
smuggled in through a cell.

The order of the chapters is the order the problems arrive in. Text first,
because untidy text is how most tables greet you; then conversions, because a
cleaned column is often still the wrong kind; then dates, the conversion with
its own vocabulary; then the conditional; then missing values last, because
missingness touches everything before it.
